description: We are a team of five passionate, curious, and multidisciplinary individuals with a shared love for technology, AI, and innovation. Combining our skills in AI, information technology, and application development, we aim to think beyond boundaries, turn bold ideas into meaningful solutions, and create something impactful through NASA Space Apps. We dream big, collaborate, and aren't afraid to explore the unknown!
summary:
The Great Mars Detective Club is a free 3D browser game for students aged 9 to 14. The player is Captain Pebble, a young space detective who explores Mars with a robot sidekick called Ziggy to solve Case #001: "Did Mars ever have water?"

The answer is not given to the player. They find three real NASA machines that are still on Mars (the Viking 1 lander, the Opportunity rover and the Phoenix lander), scan each one, read its case file, and repeat the experiment that machine actually ran. Each machine gives one Evidence Card. On the final case board the player puts the clues in time order and reaches an honest verdict: Mars had liquid water long ago and has ice today, but nobody yet knows whether life existed there.

This addresses the challenge directly. For each machine the game tells what it was, why NASA sent it, how it worked, what it discovered and why it stopped. It matters because these machines are usually remembered as abandoned hardware. The game shows students that their discoveries still shape what we know about Mars, and it lets them practice reasoning from evidence instead of memorizing facts.
details:
The Great Mars Detective Club is a free 3D browser game that turns NASA's abandoned Mars machines into a detective story for kids aged 9 to 14.

WHAT IT DOES

The player is Captain Pebble, a young space detective who lands on Mars with a robot sidekick called Ziggy to solve Case #001: "Did Mars ever have water?" The clues are three real machines that NASA left behind: the Viking 1 lander, the Opportunity rover and the Phoenix lander.

The player walks across the Martian surface, finds each machine and scans it. Each scan opens a short "memory" told by Ziggy: what the machine was sent to do, what it found, and how its mission ended. Then the player does the machine's job in a hands-on mini activity:

- Soil Lab (Viking 1): test soil samples the way the lander did.

- Rock Scanner (Opportunity): scan rocks and spot the ones that carry water clues, like the tiny mineral "blueberries".

- Dig Site (Phoenix): dig a trench and uncover the bright ice Phoenix found under the soil.

Each activity unlocks an Evidence Card. With all three cards, the player opens the Case Board, connects the evidence and gives the verdict. A journal keeps every fact and card, and a side mission lets the player collect scrap to repair their toolbox.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Discarded equipment on Mars is usually described as junk. Our game shows children that these machines are witnesses: each one still tells part of the story of water on Mars. Players learn by doing the science in the same order scientists did it (observe, test, collect evidence, conclude), so they practise the scientific method while they play, and no single machine gives the full answer.

The game runs in any modern browser with nothing to install and no account, so a teacher can open it in a classroom or a child can play it at home. Short sentences, a friendly guide and a 10 to 15 minute case keep it accessible for young readers.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Languages: TypeScript, CSS

- Framework: Next.js 15 and React 19, exported as a static website

- 3D: Three.js through React Three Fiber and Drei, with Rapier physics

- State and UI: Zustand, Tailwind CSS, Motion for animation

- Content: all story text, facts and activities are stored in JSON files, separate from the code, so they are easy to check and correct

- Assets: official NASA 3D models of the Viking lander and Opportunity rover, NASA mission photos, and a stylized Phoenix model built in code

- Hardware: ordinary laptops; the game needs only a keyboard and mouse

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a timeline or a gallery, we turned mission history into a mystery with one question a child cares about answering. The machines are the witnesses, the mini activities are the interrogation, and the Evidence Cards are the proof. The player becomes the investigator and reaches the conclusion themselves. The loading screen, characters and interface are drawn in one warm cartoon style so Mars feels like a place to explore, not a lesson.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: every fact in the game is logged against a NASA or JPL source in SOURCES.md in our repository. Where NASA pages disagree on a date, we left the date out of the game.

- Honesty about uncertainty: Viking 1's results are presented as a puzzle scientists still discuss, not as a simple answer.

- Age fit: reading level, short sessions, clear goals and no failure states that punish the player.

- Access: works in the browser, no install, no login, no personal data collected.

- Respect for NASA media: photos and models are credited in the game, and the game states that it is not endorsed by NASA.
dataRefs: JPL: Bright Chunks at Phoenix Lander’s Mars Site Must Have Been Ice
